Density is how heavy something is compared to how big it is. If an object is very heavy for its size, it has high density. If it is light for its size, it has low density.

Heat changes density. When something gets hotter, its density usually goes down because the atoms move more and spread out. When it gets cooler, its density usually goes up because the atoms move slower and pack together. Most materials follow this rule, but some do not. Water is one of those. When water turns into ice, it becomes lighter and floats.

People use fresh water as a standard to measure how dense other things are. This is called specific gravity.

The common units to measure density are grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³) and kilograms per cubic meter (kg/m³). If the number on the left (grams or kilograms) is much bigger than the number on the right (cubic centimeters or cubic meters), the material is denser. If the number on the right is bigger, the material is less dense.

Rivers and streams serve not merely as conduits for water, but also as pathways for sediment. As water flows over the bed of a channel, it mobilizes and transports sediment downstream in forms such as bed load, suspended load, or dissolved load.
